digest.top_line: Brantsch prospective cSCC cohort (n=615): 0/207 metastases at ≤2.0 mm thickness vs 16% >6.0 mm; desmoplasia drove local recurrence (HR 16.11) after clear-margin surgery alone.
digest.tldr: Skin-only day. Four retrospective nasal/facial BCC/SCC RT series (kV, orthovoltage, HDR contact and plesiotherapy) report 5y local control or cure 85-93%. The nose and the field margin are where they fail. The prospective Brantsch surgery-alone cohort names thickness >6.0 mm and desmoplasia as the risk factors for selecting adjuvant RT.

sites.intro: Mostly single-institution retrospective RT series without a comparator. Short follow-up and treating-team cosmesis grading limit every one.

studies.name: Kilovoltage RT for skin carcinomas over nasal cartilage (671 lesions)
studies.tldr: 5-yr cure 88.09%, 10-yr 86.51% after kV RT for 671 nasal BCC/SCC lesions; 96.84% good/acceptable cosmesis, no complications reported.
details: 🔍 Retrospective single-series, 671 BCC and SCC lesions over nasal cartilage, treated 1972–2007
💊 Kilovoltage RT: 668 lesions conventional roentgentherapy (CRT), 3 HDRT + CRT

subdetails: 55–60 kV, 4–6 mA, no filter, HVD 2–12 mm
Field margin 0.5–1 cm; 1.5 cm for 20 morpheaform BCCs
Ala nasi: 1 mm Pb lead rubber nostril shield to protect septal cartilage

details: 📊 Recurrence onset 3–96 mo (mean 37.96 mo); 37 of 38 relapses were BCC
📐 No statistically significant link between relapse risk and dose or lesion size
📊 No complications or sequelae to RT observed to date
⚠️ Mean f/u 38.016 mo (range 1–351) roughly equals mean time to relapse; late failures likely undercounted
⚠️ 25 of 38 recurrences marginal: field margin, not dose, is the visible failure mode
⚠️ Cosmesis graded by treating team, no validated scale; no stats on dose vs cosmesis (sample too inhomogeneous)
⚠️ 'Superior to any other modality' rests on literature comparison, not a controlled comparator
🔗 Authors cite a randomized facial BCC trial in which surgery outperformed RT for lesions <4 cm, with mixed RT techniques

verdict.rationale: Uncontrolled retrospective series spanning 35 years, short mean follow-up, investigator-graded cosmesis; cannot support the authors' superiority claim over surgery.
verdict.audience: BCC/SCC of skin overlying nasal cartilage

studies.significance: Failure pattern is the RT read: 25 of 38 recurrences were marginal, with no dose or size relationship across 30–75 Gy at 5 Gy/fx. That argues field margin (0.5–1 cm, 1.5 cm for morpheaform) gates control more than total dose, supporting moderate-dose hypofractionated kV with generous margins and nostril shielding at the ala.
studies.monday_clinic: In a pt with BCC or SCC over nasal cartilage who declines or is a poor candidate for excision, this supports kilovoltage RT as a cartilage-sparing curative option; it does not establish equivalence to surgical excision.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Retrospective** series of **671 BCC and SCC lesions** over the nasal cartilage, treated with kilovoltage RT 1972–2007. Actuarial cure rate by life-table method; mean follow-up **38.016 mo** (range 1–351).

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: 668 lesions treated with CRT at **55–60 kV**, **5 Gy/fx twice weekly**, total **30–75 Gy** (median 55 Gy); 3 lesions HDRT + CRT. Margin **0.5–1 cm**, **1.5 cm** for morpheaform BCC; 1 mm Pb nostril shield at the ala nasi.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: CR 663 (98.80%) at 1 mo; **5-yr cure 88.09%**, **10-yr 86.51%**. 38 recurrences (5.66%), **25 marginal** and 13 central, onset 3–96 mo.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: **No complications or sequelae** reported. Cosmesis good 74.47%, acceptable 22.37%, not acceptable 2.40%; the not-acceptable group is flagged for ongoing monitoring.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The authors cite randomized facial BCC data in which surgery gave better control than RT for lesions <4 cm, with similar cosmesis at the nose after 4 years; that trial mixed brachytherapy, contact and conventional RT. This series offers no internal surgical comparator.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents BCC and SCC confined to skin overlying nasal cartilage, treated with superficial kV RT. Does not represent lesions invading bone or cartilage, or nasal vestibule tumors the authors route to higher energy or interstitial techniques.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Mean follow-up roughly equals the mean time to recurrence (37.96 mo), so late failures are likely undercounted. Cosmesis was investigator-graded without a validated scale, and treatment spans 35 years of evolving staging and technique.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The predominance of **marginal** over central failures, with no dose-response signal, points to field definition as the main modifiable factor. Most relapses were salvaged non-surgically, mostly with topical 5-FU.

studies.interpretation:
The core value of this series is size and anatomic focus. Skin carcinoma over the nasal cartilage is a site where surgery is technically constrained, because the skin is tethered to cartilage and an adequate margin often forces a flap or graft, and where RT has long been considered a classic indication. A 671-lesion experience with a 5-year actuarial cure rate of 88.09% and a 10-year rate of 86.51% is a reasonable reference point for counselling a pt who would rather avoid reconstruction. The absence of reported cartilage complications at 5 Gy per fraction, despite a historical concern about chondritis with kV beams over cartilage, is the more practically reassuring finding.

Confidence should be tempered in three directions. First, follow-up: a mean of 38.016 months is barely longer than the mean time to recurrence of 37.96 months, and relapses appeared as late as 96 months. The crude recurrence figure of 5.66% is therefore a floor, and the actuarial 10-year number rests on a thinning tail. Second, outcome ascertainment: cosmesis was graded by the treating group on a three-tier scale tied to atrophy, dyschromia and telangiectasia, with no blinded or pt-reported assessment, and the authors could not test dose against cosmesis because the sample was too inhomogeneous. Third, the series spans 1972 to 2007, so staging, histologic subtyping and field definition practices drifted across the cohort.

The pattern-of-failure data carry the most transferable signal for an RT reader. Of 38 recurrences, 25 were marginal and 13 central, and the authors found no statistically significant relationship between relapse and either total dose (30–75 Gy) or lesion size. Read together, that suggests the binding constraint is target definition rather than dose, consistent with the authors' own move to a 1.5 cm margin for morpheaform BCC because its edge is hard to judge clinically. A department using tight 0.5 cm margins on infiltrative histology should take that as the cautionary point.

The conclusion that kV RT is superior to every other modality does not follow from these data. The only randomized evidence the authors cite, in facial BCC, favored surgery for control in lesions under 4 cm, while showing comparable cosmesis specifically at the nose; this uncontrolled series cannot overturn that. What it does support is narrower: for nasal skin carcinoma confined to skin over cartilage, moderate-dose hypofractionated superficial RT gives durable control in most lesions, salvageable failures, and acceptable cosmesis without reported cartilage damage. Whether it matches margin-controlled excision at this site remains untested here, and would need a contemporary comparative cohort with longer, independently assessed follow-up.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Failure pattern is the RT read: 25 of 38 recurrences were marginal, with no dose or size relationship across 30–75 Gy at 5 Gy/fx. Field margin (0.5–1 cm, 1.5 cm for morpheaform) looks like the lever, alongside nostril shielding at the ala.

open_questions: Control vs margin-controlled excision at the nasal cartilage site
Late recurrence and cosmesis beyond 5 years
Optimal field margin for infiltrative histology

studies.name: Hypofractionated HDR plesiotherapy in nonmelanoma skin cancer
studies.tldr: 5y DFS 93.36% overall (Leipzig 94.9% vs mold 88%) with 3 Gy/fx HDR surface brachy across 134 BCC/SCC lesions; recurrent lesions fared worse.
details: 🔍 Retrospective single-institution series: 114 pts, 134 lesions (92 BCC, 42 SCC), Nov 2006 to Dec 2011
🔍 All clinically N0; analysis per tumor, not per patient

subdetails: Adjuvant after excision with positive/close margins: 32 lesions (22.7%; 17 BCC, 15 SCC)
Mean dose 48.79 Gy (45-54) BCC; 50.55 Gy (45-57) SCC
PTV = lesion + 0.5-1 cm margin; dose prescribed 3-5 mm below skin
Leipzig 2- or 3-cm applicator for flat lesions ≤2 cm (101 lesions, 75.4%)
CT-planned custom wax/plaster mold for raised surfaces or lesions >2 cm

details: 📊 Complete regression 98%; no regional or distant metastases
📊 BCC 3y/5y DFS 94.1%/91.3%; all 6 BCC failures after Leipzig applicators
📊 SCC: 2 local relapses (4.8%), 3y and 5y DFS 97.5% at median f/u 35 mo

subdetails: Definitive vs adjuvant: OR 2.928 (95% CI 1.287-6.659), p=0.013

details: 📊 Late G0-1 in 120 cases (95.2%); one G4 ulcer (0.8%)
📊 Cosmesis excellent/good 82%, fair 13%, not available 5%
⚠️ Applicator chosen by lesion size and contour, so the mold vs Leipzig comparison is confounded by size
⚠️ Internal inconsistency: 'six local recurrences (five Leipzig and three molds)' does not add up
⚠️ Acute ≥G2 reported as 57.3% in abstract vs G1-2 57.5% in results; G3 40.3% is high for 3 Gy/fx
⚠️ Toxicity OR 2.25 called borderline (p=0.067) though its CI 1.012-5.003 excludes 1
⚠️ Median f/u 33 mo is short for 5y DFS claims in BCC, where late recurrence is common

verdict.rationale: Retrospective single-center series; applicator assigned by lesion size, so the technique comparison is confounded. Inconsistent recurrence and toxicity counts; 33-mo median f/u.
verdict.audience: Clinically N0 BCC/SCC, definitive or adjuvant (close/positive margin)

studies.significance: The RT-relevant read is disease status, not applicator: recurrent lesions reached only 85.9% 5y DFS vs 95.6% for primaries (p=0.003). Acute G3 was 40.3% at 3 Gy x3/week, and definitive treatment carried higher acute toxicity than adjuvant (OR 2.928). Counsel recurrent and definitive-intent pts accordingly.
studies.monday_clinic: For a clinically N0 recurrent BCC or SCC referred for HDR surface brachytherapy, this series sets lower local-control expectations than for primary lesions. It does not address lesions >2 cm on flat surfaces treated with alternatives such as electrons or electronic brachytherapy.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Retrospective** single-institution series, **114 pts / 134 lesions**, treated Nov 2006 to Dec 2011. Analysis per tumor; median follow-up **33 mo**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **92 BCC, 42 SCC**, all **clinically N0**. 77.3% definitive; 22.7% adjuvant after excision with **positive or close margins**.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Ir-192 HDR plesiotherapy, **3 Gy/fx, 3 fx/week**; mean **48.79 Gy** (BCC) and **50.55 Gy** (SCC). PTV = lesion + 0.5-1 cm, prescribed 3-5 mm deep; **Leipzig 2-3 cm** for flat lesions ≤2 cm, **CT-planned custom mold** for raised or >2 cm lesions.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Overall 3y/5y DFS **95.12% / 93.36%**, complete regression **98%**. Recurrent disease did worse (5y DFS **85.9% vs 95.6%**, p=0.003); definitive vs adjuvant showed no DFS difference (94.86% vs 96.3%, p=0.412).

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Acute RTOG G3 **40.3%**, G4 2.2%; definitive intent raised acute toxicity (OR 2.928, p=0.013). Late G0-1 **95.2%**; one G4 ulcer in a 40-mm recurrent leg SCC with venous insufficiency after 54 Gy. Cosmesis excellent/good **82%**.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The authors place their results alongside the Kohler Leipzig-applicator and Guix custom-mold series, and describe their 5y DFS as favorable against the RT arm of the only randomized surgery vs RT trial. Mohs surgery keeps the lowest recurrence rates in the cited literature.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents clinically N0 BCC and SCC treated with moderately hypofractionated HDR surface brachytherapy, definitive or margin-positive adjuvant. Does not represent node-positive, perineural or high-risk cutaneous SCC, or melanoma.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Event and toxicity counts conflict internally (five plus three recurrences reported as six; acute ≥G2 57.3% vs G1-2 57.5%). The 33-mo median follow-up is short for BCC, where late recurrence is common. No pt-reported cosmesis.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The series supports HDR plesiotherapy as a valid non-surgical option for NMSC and favors matching the applicator to lesion geometry. It cannot rank molds against Leipzig applicators, or 3 Gy/fx against other schedules.

studies.interpretation:
The question this series actually answers is narrower than its title. It shows that a single department delivering 3 Gy fractions three times weekly, through either a rigid Leipzig cup or a CT-planned custom mold, gets local control in the low-to-mid 90s at roughly three years for clinically node-negative BCC and SCC. That is the range a radiation oncologist would expect from surface brachytherapy, and it is in line with the Kohler and Guix experiences the authors cite. What the series does not answer is the comparative question it sets itself, which technique is better. Applicator choice was decided by the lesion itself: flat lesions of 2 cm or less went into the Leipzig cup, while raised or larger lesions got a mold. Molds treated lesions averaging 19.38 vs 13.07 mm. Any difference in control or toxicity between the two arms is therefore inseparable from size and anatomic contour. The authors partly acknowledge this by re-running statistics restricted to Leipzig-range sizes, but the excerpt does not report clean results from that restricted comparison.

The more useful signal for practice is disease status. Recurrent lesions held 85.9% DFS at both 3 and 5 years, against 97.9% and 95.6% for primaries, and this was the one prognostic split that reached p=0.003. A recurrent BCC or SCC has already escaped one local therapy and is plausibly deeper or more infiltrative than its clinical margins suggest. A dose prescribed 3 to 5 mm below the surface with a 0.5 to 1 cm margin may undertreat such a lesion. That fits a reasonable hypothesis that surface brachytherapy depth and margin conventions designed for primary disease are not automatically adequate for recurrent disease, although this series is too small to test it.

The toxicity data deserve more scepticism than the control data. An acute G3 rate of 40.3% is high for a schedule the authors call moderate hypofractionation, and their own discussion describes acute rates as lower than the 10 to 21% elsewhere, a claim hard to square with their numbers unless the scales or denominators differ. The abstract and results also disagree on the acute ≥G2 figure, the recurrence tally does not sum, and an odds ratio with a confidence interval excluding 1 is reported as only borderline. None of these overturns the headline, but together they lower confidence in the secondary comparisons. A reader should treat the applicator and size-related toxicity findings as descriptive.

Late toxicity and cosmesis are reassuring: 95.2% late G0-1, 82% excellent or good cosmesis, and a single G4 ulcer in a lower-extremity SCC with venous insufficiency. That case is the familiar warning about treating the lower leg with compromised vascular supply, not a signal against the technique.

For positioning, this belongs with the broader single-institution brachytherapy literature: favorable control, acceptable cosmesis, no randomized comparator against excision, Mohs, electrons or electronic brachytherapy, and follow-up too short to capture late BCC recurrence. It supports offering HDR plesiotherapy to pts who are poor surgical candidates or who decline surgery, especially for primary lesions in cosmetically sensitive sites. It does not establish 3 Gy x3/week as a preferred schedule. It also does not say which applicator to choose beyond the obvious rule of matching geometry to the surface.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Disease status, not applicator, separates outcomes: recurrent lesions reached 85.9% 5y DFS vs 95.6% for primaries (p=0.003). With acute G3 at 40.3% on 3 Gy x3/week and higher acute toxicity for definitive treatment (OR 2.928), this informs depth, margin and counselling for recurrent and definitive-intent lesions.

open_questions: HDR plesiotherapy vs excision, Mohs or electrons in a randomized comparison
Optimal fractionation for HDR skin brachytherapy
Dose or margin escalation for recurrent NMSC

studies.name: Radiotherapy for nasal skin SCC, Princess Margaret experience
studies.tldr: Local failure-free rate 90% at 2y and 85% at 5y with mostly hypofractionated orthovoltage RT for nasal skin SCC; CSS 96%, no G4 late toxicity.
details: 🔍 Retrospective single-institution chart review, 1982-1993; 100 referred, 94 assessable (6 lost to f/u)
🔍 T1 60, T2 11, T3 0, T4 7, TX 16; only 1 pt node-positive at presentation
🔍 RT alone 63 (67%); surgery then postop RT 31 (33%)

subdetails: Submandibular nodal failure after surgical primary control: n=1
>5 cm or bone/cartilage invasion: 50 Gy/20 fx

details: 🔍 Modality: orthovoltage 76 (81%), electrons 13 (14%), cobalt 4 (4%), MV photons 1

details.text: 📊 Actuarial outcomes from start of RT
📊 Local failures (n=10) by site and pattern
subdetails: Bridge 6, columella 2, side of nose to cheek/canthus 1, tip 1
Relapse after no gross disease: 3 marginal, 2 in-field, 1 both

details: 📊 No elective nodal RT; regional failure in only 2 of 93 pts without nodes at presentation
📊 Salvage in 8 pts (surgery 4, re-RT 4); 5 disease-free at last f/u
📊 No RTOG G4 late toxicity; no cartilage or bone necrosis despite 81% orthovoltage
⚠️ Late toxicity and cosmesis not formally scored
⚠️ Univariate analysis found no prognostic factor; only 10 local failure events
🔗 vs Mazeron et al. (1676 nose/vestibule skin cases): 11% local failure in SCC, similar to 10% at 2y here

verdict.rationale: Single-institution retrospective series with no comparator. Size-driven, heterogeneous schedules prevent any dose-response read. Median f/u in survivors only 2.9 y.
verdict.audience: Nasal skin SCC (not vestibule), mostly T1N0, primary or postop RT

studies.significance: Failures cluster where tumor extent is easy to underestimate: 6 of 10 local failures were on the bridge, 3 of 4 bridge recurrences after CR had a marginal component, and 2 of 5 columella lesions failed. That argues for generous margins (1 cm to field edge was typical) and careful depth estimation at those sites.
studies.monday_clinic: In an elderly pt with nasal skin SCC who wants a short course, this supports a 1-2 week hypofractionated schedule with accepted late cosmetic cost; it does not extend to nasal vestibule SCC, which was excluded.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Retrospective chart review**, single institution (Princess Margaret), pts treated 1982-1993. **94 of 100** assessable after 6 lost to follow-up. Median follow-up in the 45 survivors **2.9 y** (range 0.2-10.4).

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Histologically confirmed **SCC of nasal skin**; **nasal vestibule SCC excluded**. T1 60, T2 11, T4 7, TX 16; 1 pt N1. RT judged treatment of choice at multidisciplinary review; 63 RT alone, 31 postop for gross residual (15) or positive margin (15).

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **81% orthovoltage** (75-250 keV), 14% electrons (9-20 MeV, bolus always), 4% cobalt. Typical schedules **35 Gy/5** (<2 cm), **45 Gy/10** (2-5 cm), **50 Gy/20** (>5 cm or bone/cartilage invasion). Primary lesion only, **no intentional nodal coverage**; margin of 1 cm to field edge typical.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** local failure-free rate. Secondary: nodal failure-free rate, OS, cause-specific survival, late toxicity.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Local failure-free rate **90% at 2y, 85% at 5y**; CSS 96% at both. 10 local failures, 6 on the bridge.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: **No RTOG G4 late toxicity** and no cartilage or bone necrosis. Skin pallor, atrophy and telangiectasia common 1-5 y after RT, progressive but usually asymptomatic.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Mazeron et al. reported **11% local failure** for SCC across 1676 nose and vestibule skin cancers, in line with the **10% 2y local failure** here. Mazeron also found vestibule and columella tumors failed more often (24%) than other external nose sites (5%), matching the columella signal here.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents nasal skin SCC, mostly T1N0, treated with primary or postop RT to the primary only. Does not represent nasal vestibule SCC, which was excluded and carries worse outcomes.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Late toxicity and **cosmesis were never formally scored**, so the schedule vs cosmetic trade-off is anecdotal. With **10 local failures**, the null univariate analysis is underpowered. Orthovoltage-era technique (1982-1993) and mixed definitive/postop cohorts limit transfer.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Authors' current preference is **50 Gy/20** or **60 Gy/30** for large infiltrative lesions, since most pts on <4-week schedules show a visible cosmetic defect after 1-2 y. Many elderly pts still choose 1-2 week courses and accept the cosmetic cost. Optimal fractionation **cannot be derived** from this series.

studies.interpretation:
This series remains one of the cleaner single-institution reads on definitive and postoperative RT for nasal skin SCC, and its main contribution is less the headline control rate than where and how the failures happened. A 2y local failure rate of 10% sits close to the 11% Mazeron et al. reported for squamous lesions in a much larger nose and vestibule series. Two independent cohorts landing near the same number makes the control estimate believable for a selected, mostly T1N0 population. What it does not do is say how RT compares with excision or Mohs. Every pt here was judged an RT candidate at multidisciplinary review, so the cohort is defined by referral, not by randomization.

The failure pattern is the more transferable finding. Six of the ten local failures were on the nasal bridge, three of the four bridge recurrences after an initial complete response had a marginal component, and two of the five columella lesions failed. The authors read this as underestimated tumor extent on curved surfaces and along embryonic fusion planes, and Mazeron's higher failure rate at the columella and vestibule points the same way. For a radiation oncologist that turns into a planning instruction more than a dose instruction: on the bridge and columella, the margin and the depth estimate are what fail, not the dose itself. The series cannot test a dose-response relationship, because dose was chosen by lesion size and depth, and the null univariate analysis rests on ten events.

The nodal data support the long-standing practice of treating the primary only. Only one pt presented node-positive, and two of the remaining 93 developed regional failure without elective coverage, and neither case could be predicted in retrospect from features of the primary. That backs surveillance over elective nodal RT for cN0 disease, though the series is far too small to identify the minority who would benefit, and the immunosuppressed subset (five pts, one nodal failure) is anecdotal.

The toxicity claim needs more caution than the abstract suggests. The absence of RTOG G4 late effects and of cartilage or bone necrosis with mostly orthovoltage beams is reassuring about the theoretical concern of higher bone dose. But late toxicity and cosmesis were never formally scored, so 'well tolerated' means that no severe event reached the chart. The authors' own move from 35 Gy/5 and 45 Gy/10 toward 50 Gy/20 is an implicit admission that cosmesis on short schedules was worse than the control data alone reveal.

The decision this informs is the fractionation conversation with an elderly pt. The series supports offering a 1-2 week course with an honest discussion of later cosmetic cost, and a longer course when cosmesis matters more than visit burden, with no evidence that either choice costs local control. For this to be wrong, the short-schedule control would have to degrade with longer follow-up than these survivors reached, which a 2.9 y median cannot exclude.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Failures cluster on the bridge (6 of 10) and columella (2 of 5 failed), with 3 of 4 bridge recurrences after CR marginal. That moves margin and depth estimation at those sites, not dose; primary-only fields held, with 2 of 93 regional failures.

open_questions: Optimal dose-fractionation balancing cosmesis and local control
Better margin and depth definition for bridge and columella lesions
Which cN0 nasal SCC pts warrant elective nodal RT

studies.name: Brantsch cSCC prognostic risk factors (prospective, n=615)
studies.tldr: No metastases at ≤2.0 mm thickness (0/207); >6.0 mm metastasized in 16%, and desmoplasia drove local recurrence (HR 16.11) after clear-margin surgery.
details: 🔍 Prospective single-centre cohort (Tübingen), 653 enrolled, 615 assessable, 1990-2001
🔍 All pts resected with complete 3D-histology margin control; all margins tumour-free
🔍 No pt received adjuvant RT: this is a surgery-alone natural history
📊 Median f/u 43 mo; 26 (4%) metastases, 20 (3%) local recurrences

details.text: 📐 Best multivariate Cox model, independent factors (HR, 95% CI)

details: 📊 Desmoplastic SCC: local recurrence 12/51 (24%) vs 8/564 (1%) non-desmoplastic
🔍 Perineural or perivascular invasion was always accompanied by desmoplasia in this series

details.text: 📐 Discrimination: thickness-based best model vs current TNM model (C-index)

details: 📊 First metastasis always regional nodal; 19 within year 1, none after year 4
⚠️ Events per variable 26:7 (mets) and 20:7 (LR), below the accepted floor of 5
⚠️ White pts only, university referral centre; 38 lost to follow-up

verdict.rationale: Single-centre prospective cohort with events-per-variable below 5 for both models; wide CIs and internal-only validation limit the multivariate ranking, though thickness strata are consistent.
verdict.audience: Resected primary cutaneous SCC, clear 3D-histology margins, no adjuvant RT

studies.significance: No pt received adjuvant RT and every margin was clear, so this is the surgery-alone baseline adjuvant RT is weighed against: desmoplastic SCC (where all PNI sat) recurred locally in 12/51 (24%), and >6.0 mm tumours metastasized in 14/90 (16%), always first to regional nodes.
studies.monday_clinic: In a resected primary cSCC with clear margins and thickness ≤2.0 mm, this series recorded no metastases in 207 pts, supporting no adjuvant treatment discussion on risk grounds; it does not extend to positive margins or recurrent tumours treated elsewhere.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Prospective single-centre observational cohort (STROBE), Tübingen, surgery **1990-2001**, follow-up closed Dec 2005. **653 enrolled, 615 assessable**; median f/u **43 mo** (range 1-165).

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: White pts with **primary cutaneous SCC** of any body site, median age 73, 63% men. Excluded SCC in situ, keratoacanthoma, collision tumours and **recurrent SCC treated elsewhere**; 31 immunosuppressed.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **No pt received adjuvant RT.** Resection used 2-10 mm safety margins with 3D-histology, re-excised until **completely tumour-free margins** in all pts.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** time to metastasis and time to local recurrence from primary diagnosis. Seven a priori candidate predictors entered Cox models with forward selection.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Thickness stratified risk cleanly: **0/207 metastases at ≤2.0 mm**, 16% above 6.0 mm. **Desmoplasia** was the dominant local-recurrence factor (**HR 16.11**).

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The contemporaneous AJCC/UICC TNM staged cSCC by horizontal size and differentiation, with depth only for extradermal invasion. The thickness model discriminated better (**C-index 0.837 vs 0.743** for mets); poor differentiation failed validation.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents primary cSCC resected to clear margins under 3D-histology without adjuvant RT. Does not represent positive-margin, recurrent, or heavily immunosuppressed transplant-type populations.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Immunosuppression defined by chemotherapy or other malignancy, only 31 pts, so transplant risk is not characterized. Follow-up partly by physician questionnaire, and the index tumour in multi-SCC pts was assigned retrospectively.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Authors propose thickness-based T1 (≤2.0 mm), T2 (2.1-6.0 mm), T3 (>6.0 mm) with **d** and **i** suffixes, and nodal ultrasound every 3 or 4 months for 4 years in high-risk pts. The SLNB and adjuvant-therapy questions are explicitly left open.

studies.interpretation:
This cohort has mattered for longer than its sample size would predict because it fixed the depth of invasion as the axis along which cutaneous SCC risk actually separates. The tumour-size and Broders-grade framework it was compared against treated depth as relevant only once extradermal structures were breached. Here, depth beat both: poor differentiation dropped out on validation, with an HR of 0.72 in the 415-pt validation sample, and horizontal size only made the metastasis model as a weaker co-variable. Later staging systems moved toward depth, and this paper is one of the reasons.

For a radiation oncologist the most useful property is easy to miss: nobody received adjuvant RT, and every margin was cleared by 3D-histology with repeated topographic re-excision. That makes the event rates a surgery-alone baseline under close to ideal margin control. A local recurrence rate of 3% overall, and 1% once desmoplastic tumours are removed, is the floor any adjuvant RT argument has to clear. Pts with thin, non-desmoplastic tumours leave essentially nothing for adjuvant treatment to improve. Pts with desmoplastic histology, where every case of perineural invasion in this series also sat, are a different matter: 12 of 51 recurred locally despite clear margins. That is the subgroup where the local adjuvant question is most alive, and the study cannot answer it because it never tested RT.

The pattern-of-failure data sharpen the nodal question. The first metastasis was always regional nodal, most occurred in the first year, and none occurred after year four. That supports the authors' proposal of intensive nodal surveillance for high-risk pts, and it frames the alternatives a radiation oncologist would raise for tumours above 6.0 mm or in immunosuppressed pts: observation with ultrasound, SLNB, or elective nodal treatment. None of those arms exists here.

Confidence in the multivariate ranking should be modest. The authors state the events-per-variable ratio fell below the accepted floor of five for both endpoints and that a sample over three times larger would be needed. Hazard ratios such as 16.11 for desmoplasia carry intervals spanning several-fold, and the learning and validation split was internal. What survives this weakness is the univariate gradient by thickness, which is large, monotonic, and reproduced in both samples; the precise ordering of immunosuppression, ear location and size is far less secure.

Transfer is the other caveat. These are white pts from a single German referral centre with 3D-histology margins, so a practice relying on standard excision with bread-loafed margins would likely see higher local failure across every stratum. The result would be wrong in its practical reading if the near-zero metastatic rate below 2.0 mm reflected margin technique or referral mix rather than biology, which this design cannot separate.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: This is the surgery-alone baseline with clear margins and no adjuvant RT: desmoplastic SCC (all PNI cases) still recurred locally in 12/51 (24%), and >6.0 mm tumours metastasized in 16%, always first to regional nodes. Those strata define where an adjuvant local or nodal RT discussion has room to help.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: With 3D-histology clearing every margin, local recurrence was 1% in non-desmoplastic tumours, so margin technique carries most of the local-control load. Thickness >6.0 mm and immunosuppression flag the nodal basin, the first metastatic site in every case, as the SLNB and ultrasound-surveillance question the authors leave open.

studies.name: HDR contact brachytherapy with customized molds for facial cutaneous carcinoma
studies.tldr: 5y actuarial LC 89% for ≤3 mm thick facial BCC/SCC: 100% on flat skin, 83% on nose, with nasal tip failing 4 of 15.
details: 🔍 Retrospective, single institution (Valencia), 51 facial lesions in 48 pts, treated 1999 to 2005

subdetails: Thickness ≤3 mm in all; thicker lesions went to electrons

details.text: 💊 Ir-192 HDR contact fractionation used (3 fx/wk)

details: 🔍 Standard schedule 48 Gy in 12 fx of 4 Gy, overall time 4 weeks
📐 Prescribed 3 mm below skin, 1 cm margin; skin surface usually around 150% of dose, never more
🔍 Nasal lesions: wax molds, CT-planned; flat surfaces: 0.5 cm bolus with tubes 1 cm apart
📊 Local control by subsite
📊 Actuarial LC 91% at 2y, 89% at 5y and 8y; median f/u 45 mo (range 4-102)
📊 5 relapses (9.8%) at 6-32 mo: 3 in-field, 2 at field border
⚠️ All 5 relapses were on the nose and all had used only 3 catheters
📊 All relapses salvaged by surgery; no nodal or distant spread, no cancer deaths

subdetails: G1-2 dermatitis: 30 pts (78%), resolved in days
G4 dermatitis: 11 pts (21%), healed in 3 weeks as outpatients
No late complications reported, including no nasal chondritis
Cosmesis good or very good in all cases

details: ⚠️ G4 dermatitis rate is internally inconsistent: 21% in Results, 12% in Discussion
🔗 vs Guix et al contact HDR-BT (136 lesions, 60-65 Gy at 1.8 Gy/session): 5y actuarial LC 98%
⚠️ Three schedules applied without protocol assignment, so no dose-response read is possible

verdict.rationale: Retrospective single-institution series of 51 lesions with no comparator arm and clinician-chosen fractionation across three schedules.
verdict.audience: Facial BCC/SCC ≤3 mm thick, ≤4 cm, median age 78

studies.significance: The failure was geometric: all 5 relapses were on the nose, all with 3-catheter molds, two at the field border, in tumors of only 7-20 mm. Nasal tip LC was 73% vs 95% for pyramid/wing. That changes mold design (more than three catheters, full lateral-margin coverage) and sends nasal tip lesions to another technique.
studies.monday_clinic: In a pt with a ≤3 mm thick facial BCC or SCC on the temple, forehead, cheek, or nasal pyramid/wing, this supports custom-mold HDR contact brachy as an alternative to surgery or electrons; it does not extend to nasal tip lesions or thicker tumors.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Retrospective**, single institution (Fundación IVO, Valencia), 51 lesions in 48 pts treated January 1999 to November 2005. Median follow-up **45 mo** (range 4-102).

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Facial BCC (82.4%) and SCC (17.6%), mean diameter 1.5 cm (0.5-4 cm). **Thickness ≤3 mm** was the gate; thicker lesions were treated with electrons. Radical intent in 95%, adjuvant for involved lateral margin in 5%.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Ir-192 HDR contact brachy via custom wax molds (nose) or 0.5 cm bolus (flat skin), **1 cm margin**, prescribed **3 mm below the skin**. Standard **48 Gy in 12 fx of 4 Gy** over 4 weeks; 37% got 51-57 Gy at 3 Gy/fx and 6% got 35 Gy in 5 fx of 7 Gy.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Actuarial LC **89% at 5y**, with **100% on flat skin** and **83% on the nose**. All relapses were nasal and all were salvaged surgically.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: G1-2 dermatitis in 78% and **G4 dermatitis in 21%**, healed within 3 weeks. **No late complications**, including no chondritis; cosmesis good or very good in all.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Guix et al, the closest contact HDR-BT series (136 lesions), reported **98% 5y LC** using 60-65 Gy at 1.8 Gy/session, a lower dose per fraction than the 4 Gy standard here. Tsao et al reported 90% 2y and 85% 5y LC with EBRT for nasal skin SCC, the range this series' nasal arm sits in.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents thin (≤3 mm) facial BCC/SCC up to 4 cm on flat skin or the nasal pyramid/wing in older pts. Does not represent nasal tip lesions or tumors thicker than 3 mm.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Prescription depth was **fixed at 3 mm** for every lesion, and the authors cannot exclude that a deeper point would have prevented failures. Toxicity is reported inconsistently (G4 dermatitis **21% vs 12%** in different sections), and cosmesis was physician-graded on an unvalidated four-level scale.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Control on flat skin is complete, so the technique's weakness is **applicator coverage on curved nasal anatomy**, not dose to the tumor center. Whether 4 Gy fractions underperform the lower dose per fraction of other HDR series remains untested.

studies.interpretation:
The central lesson of this series is geometric rather than dosimetric. Every one of the five relapses arose on the nose, every one had been planned with only three catheters, and two occurred at the field border. The relapsing tumors were small (7-20 mm), which led the authors to blame lateral-margin coverage by the applicator rather than underdosing at the center of the target. The nasal tip, where the plastic tubes do not bend enough to cover the lower face of the lesion, ran local control of 73%, while the pyramid and wing reached 95%. Read that way, the 89% five-year headline is a blend of two quite different results: complete control on flat skin across 16 lesions, and a single anatomic subsite where mold geometry is hardest to get right.

The comparison with prior work is informative but loose. The closest analogue is Guix et al, who treated 136 cutaneous carcinomas with contact HDR-BT and reported 98% actuarial five-year control, using 60-65 Gy at 1.8 Gy per session. That is a very different schedule from the 48 Gy in 4 Gy fractions used as standard here. Tsao et al reported 90% two-year and 85% five-year control for nasal skin SCC with EBRT, and the nasal cohort in this series lands in that range despite being mostly BCC, nominally the easier histology. Whether the gap to Guix reflects dose per fraction, catheter density, or case mix cannot be resolved from two retrospective series, but a department building this program would want to know which one it is.

Several methodological features should temper confidence. The design is retrospective and single-institution, and the three fractionation schedules were assigned by the clinician rather than by protocol, so the series cannot support any dose-response inference. If anything, the two border failures received 54 and 57 Gy, the upper end of the range, which supports the coverage explanation over a dose explanation. The 3 mm thickness ceiling, with thicker lesions diverted to electrons, is a selection filter that favors control. Prescription depth was fixed at 3 mm for every lesion, and the authors concede that a deeper point might have mattered. The toxicity reporting does not agree with itself: grade 4 dermatitis appears as 21% in the results and 12% in the discussion. Healing within three weeks as outpatients suggests either an unusually strict grading or a misattribution. Cosmesis was physician-graded on a four-level scale without independent review.

For the radiation oncologist, the paper supports custom-mold contact HDR as an option for thin BCC or SCC on the temple, forehead, cheek, and nasal pyramid or wing, especially in older pts for whom outpatient sessions of 5-8 minutes without anesthesia matter. It does not support this mold design on the nasal tip, and the authors themselves now use more than three catheters on nasal molds. Surgical salvage rescued every failure, which lowers the cost of a relapse without removing it. The result would be overturned by a series with more SCC, independent cosmetic assessment, and consistent toxicity grading showing that flat-surface control falls well short of complete once selection is relaxed.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: All 5 relapses were nasal and all used 3-catheter molds, two at the field border, in small 7-20 mm tumors, so the failure mode is applicator coverage, not dose. Nasal tip LC was 73% vs 95% on pyramid/wing, which sets both mold design and subsite selection for a contact HDR program.

open_questions: Applicator design that adequately covers nasal tip lesions
Does lower dose per fraction improve control over 4 Gy fractions?
Outcomes for SCC and lesions thicker than 3 mm
